svg.title: Path isolation with VRFs on the left and security isolation with a stateful policy device on the right
svg.desc: Left panel: three VRFs, one each for OT, IT and guest, each with its own address range, RIB and adjacencies; the separation is structural because a missing route means a missing path. Right panel: what security isolation actually requires - which flows are allowed between VRFs, inspection with logging and session state, who may reach shared services, and what happens to the packet rather than only where it goes - which needs an enforcing device with state. A footer lists the four places isolation leaks: a fusion router that imports every VRF, shared services reachable from every VRF, permanent route leaking for one legacy application, and a management VRF bypassed by an out-of-band path nobody drew. The review question is to show the packet that is not allowed through and the device that drops it.
svg.text: A VRF is a separate routing table, not a policy device
Path isolation and security isolation are different products. One decides where packets can go, the other decides what they may do.
PATH ISOLATION (WHAT A VRF DOES)
VRF OT
own RIB, own adjacencies
VRF IT
own RIB, own adjacencies
VRF GUEST
own RIB, own adjacencies
two tables that never leak into each other
the separation is structural: no route, no path
SECURITY ISOLATION (WHAT A POLICY DOES)
which flows are allowed between VRFs
inspection, logging and session state
who may reach the shared services
what happens to the packet, not just where it goes
needs an enforcing device with state: firewall, or VRF-aware policy
The four places isolation leaks in real designs
1. Fusion router imports every VRF, so the tables meet and the policy was never written
2. Shared services (DNS, NTP, AD) reachable from every VRF through one interface
3. Route leaking for a legacy application that "just needs to see" one server, forever
4. Management VRF bypassed by an out-of-band path that nobody drew
The review question
"Show me the packet that is not allowed to get through,"
"and the device that drops it." If the answer is
"the VRFs are separate", nothing has been enforced.
